title: Chutes AI MCP: What It Is and How It Works (2026)
summary: Chutes AI MCP connects models to tools through the Model Context Protocol. Get implementation guidance, review costs, and understand what prevents success.
body_markdown:
## Connecting Business Apps to a Chutes Agent with Activepieces


Read-only scopes only help if something controls who can change them, and Activepieces handles that side through role-based access control: SSO and standard roles on the Team plan ($200 a month, 25 users included), custom roles and SCIM on Ultimate, so basic RBAC is accessible at the Team level.


It's the tool side of the pair, a server that hands your client a set of callable actions, and it has nothing to do with which model answers.


### Exposing workflows and integrations to clients


As an automation platform,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/blog/chutes-ai-pricing-plans-limits-and-costs-2026) can expose its workflows and its 747 integrations, counted from the MIT-licensed open source monorepo, to an MCP client as tools, meaning integration gaps are unlikely to be a limiting factor.


Your client connects to it the way it connects to any MCP server, and the model on the other end of that client can then call what you exposed.


The MCP server is included on the free plan, alongside unlimited flows, whichever model your client uses.


Below is the Agents view of the dashboard, with the MCP entry sitting in the left sidebar next to Flows, Tables and Connections. It shows two example agents, "Blog Author Enricher" and "SEO blog writer".


What to take from it is that an integration you connect in Activepieces runs two ways at once: as a step in a flow, and as a tool on the per-project MCP server.


It's the same integration action in both roles, and you can confirm that in packages/integrations in the MIT-licensed open source repo.


For a Chutes-backed client, that means nothing is wired twice.


The apps you connected for flows are already tools it can list, whether the client is Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or an agent you built yourself, and the 747 integrations come with no export step, which means you don't lose your automations when you switch clients.


A catalog you have to re-integrate for your agents is a second migration, and this one skips it. The MCP entry is the one that matters for this article.


Next comes the practical consequence. Activepieces doesn't host a model, doesn't replace Chutes, and doesn't merge billing.


Chutes still bills for inference, and with your own AI keys on Plus ($20 a month) every AI step is 1 Activepieces credit while the model cost goes to your own provider bill, so your costs are split between platform and compute provider.


Whatever the connected apps charge is a separate matter, and so is what your Activepieces plan covers: the free plan includes 1,000 credits a month and unlimited flows. Three systems, three accounts, and your client is the only thing joining them.


### When it fits and when it does not


It fits when the work you want the model to do already exists as an Activepieces flow. It also fits when you need a business app, such as a CRM or a spreadsheet, reachable without writing your own MCP server.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


You pick what to expose, and that selection is your first control over what a misread prompt can touch.


It doesn't fit if your tools already sit behind an MCP server that works.


Adding Activepieces then gives you a second hop to debug, a second set of credentials, and a second place for a tool call to fail silently, plus 1 credit for every flow run behind it, however many steps it has. Skip it.


It also fixes nothing about the model. A weak tool-calling model on Chutes stays weak with a well-built Activepieces server in front of it.
